title: Dealing With Canadian Collection Agencies
subtitle: Run the call instead of letting the call run you

blocks.text: A collection call often opens as if the caller booked your next eight minutes without checking your calendar.
You are allowed to slow it down. The first call is for gathering facts, not for making a frightened money decision before the kettle boils.

This course trains you to identify the caller, verify the account and use calm scripts. It also covers how to record what the caller does and how to pick the right complaint route. Collection law is not one national rulebook. The province, the creditor and federal regulation all matter.
A callback after you verify is a control tool. FCAC tells consumers to record the caller’s details, check their records and call back once the information is confirmed.

blocks.text: FCAC: Dealing with a debt collector
You can run a collection call instead of letting it run you.
blocks.detail: You will have a script for six common situations, so you never have to improvise under pressure.
blocks.extra: Tessa’s story comes next, then six ready-made scripts in the Respond section.

blocks.text: Meet Tessa
paragraphs: Tessa Wong works the front desk at a physiotherapy clinic in Victoria. She has an old utility account she wants to settle quietly, without dealing with it at work.
Then a collector calls during her shift. He wants an e-transfer before she leaves. When she asks for a breakdown, he talks faster. She knows the utility. She does not know the total.

Patients are arriving and her manager is nearby. Tessa does not pay, argue or share her banking details. She writes down the caller’s name, agency, number, creditor, amount and date, then says she will call back.
After work, she finds the utility’s contact details on its own website and asks for the account details in writing.
The base charge is hers. The late fee is not; it was added after her final payment. She sends the receipt, and the fee is removed. For the rest, she sets up a short schedule that matches her paydays.
Two months later, another caller demands gift cards for a tax debt. Tessa recognizes the scam, ends the call and reports it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre and local police.
She uses the same steps every time: write it down, check it herself, pay only what is correct.

blocks.text: Tessa kept three questions apart: Is the caller real? Is the account mine? Is the amount correct? Each one needed different proof.
The conclusion
Tessa paid what was valid, did not pay the error, protected her workplace and spotted a later scam. Her advantage was a process she could repeat.
You can check who is calling before you share a single detail.
blocks.detail: You will know which four facts to record and which signs mean fraud, so a confident voice never decides for you.
blocks.extra: Next, the Identify section lists what to write down before you say a word about yourself.

sections.title: Identify the Caller Before You Identify Yourself

blocks.text: A real company name on call display is not proof. Write down what the caller says, end the call if you need to and verify through contact details you find yourself.

items.title: The caller’s full name, company, phone number and mailing address.
The original creditor, the account reference, the amount claimed and the date the debt began.
A written notice, a breakdown of the balance and the agency’s role: hired collector or owner.
Your province or territory, and which consumer office oversees collectors there.

blocks.text: A written notice usually names the agency, the creditor and the amount. If the basics are missing, verify first. Do not share more.
HIGH-PRESSURE FRAUD SIGNALS
End the call if someone demands gift cards, cryptocurrency, remote access, or a banking password or PIN. End it too if they threaten arrest or refuse to let you verify.
Save the messages and report suspected fraud.

items.title: “Call display proves the caller is legitimate.”
items.text: Phone numbers on call display can be faked. Confirm the organization through official contact details before you pay or share private data.

blocks.text: Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre: Report fraud

sections.title: Use a Script That Matches the Situation

blocks.text: A script keeps the call short enough to be useful.

items.title: FIRST CONTACT
items.text: “Please give me your name, agency, phone number, original creditor, the amount you claim and the date the debt began. Send the details in writing. I will reply after I check my records.”

items.title: UNFAMILIAR DEBT
items.text: “I do not recognize this account. I am not agreeing that I owe it. Please send the creditor, the account history and the amount in writing.”

items.title: DISPUTED AMOUNT
items.text: “I know this account, but I dispute the amount because _____. I will send copies of my records. Please note the dispute and reply in writing.”

items.title: VALID BUT UNAFFORDABLE
items.text: “I cannot safely pay the full amount today. After I review my budget, I can offer a schedule in writing. I will not agree to a payment I cannot keep up.”

items.title: WRONG PERSON
items.text: “I am not the person on this account. Please fix your records and tell me in writing what you need from me through your official process.”

items.title: WORKPLACE CALL
items.text: “This workplace is not a proper place to reach me. Please note my preferred contact details and give me your reference number. I am ending this call now.”

blocks.text: Speak calmly, promise nothing you cannot keep and write down the reply.
A payment plan only works when the dates match your cash flow. Get any offer in writing and keep your receipts.

items.title: “Saying ‘I cannot pay today’ means I should avoid the debt forever.”
items.text: It means that today’s demand is not a safe plan. Verify the debt, review your essential costs and offer only terms you can keep.

blocks.text: A caution for older debts: in some places, a payment or a written acknowledgement can affect your legal rights. Get advice for your province or territory before you agree.

sections.title: Match the Complaint to the Collector

blocks.text: Start by finding out who owns the debt and who hired the collector. The right regulator depends on that relationship.

items.title: Save notices, envelopes, voicemails, screenshots, receipts and a dated call log. Write down the exact words used, with no spin.
Raise it with the agency. Give a supervisor or compliance contact the event, your concern, the fix you want and a reply date.
Contact the creditor if the agency works for one, and give them the agency’s case number.
Use your province or territory’s consumer affairs office for debt that was sold to an agency or is collected by one.
Use the financial institution’s complaint process when a federally regulated institution, or its agent, is collecting.
Report suspected scams to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre and local police. Check court papers quickly and get legal help when you need it.

blocks.text: Federal contact-time and conduct rules described by FCAC apply to federally regulated financial institutions and the parties collecting for them. Debts that were sold usually fall under provincial or territorial law.

items.title: “Every collector in Canada follows the federal bank rules.”
items.text: Which rules apply depends on how the collector and the creditor are linked, and on where you live. Check the right provincial, territorial or federal route.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: A caller gives a real bank’s name and demands payment now. What should you verify on your own?
items.detail: Verify the collector through official bank and agency contacts. Then confirm the creditor, the amount, the history and their authority.

items.title: The account is yours but the amount is wrong. Which script and proof should you use?
items.detail: Use the disputed-amount script, with copies of statements, receipts, cancellation records or other proof.

items.title: A collector for a bank uses threatening language. Where does the complaint begin?
items.detail: Save your evidence and start with the bank’s complaint process, because federal protections cover the bank and its collecting agent.

items.title: A caller demands gift cards for an alleged tax debt. What are the safe next steps?
items.detail: End the call, do not pay, verify on your own, save the evidence and report suspected fraud to the CAFC and local police.

items.title: Why can advice for your province or territory matter before you pay an old debt?
items.detail: Limitation rules differ, and a payment or written acknowledgement may affect your legal rights.

blocks.text: Verifying is not avoiding. It sorts a valid account, an error, improper conduct and a scam before you reply.

sections.title: Your Action: Collection Call Control Record

blocks.text: Fill this in from the written notice and your call notes. Keep full account numbers, passwords, PINs and ID numbers off this page.
A useful call log shows who called, when, what was said, what was promised and the next deadline. Memory rarely produces a case number six weeks later.
Control the sequence.
blocks.detail: Identify the caller, verify the account, reply in writing, document the conduct and escalate through the right jurisdiction. A real debt deserves an accurate, affordable plan. Pressure does not improve the arithmetic.

items.title: Creditor
items.text: The person or business that is owed money.

items.title: Collection agency
items.text: A business that collects unpaid debts for a creditor or, sometimes, after buying the debt.

items.title: Debt purchaser
items.text: A company that buys a debt and tries to collect it as the new owner.

items.title: Federally regulated financial institution
items.text: A bank, federal credit union or other financial institution under federal law.

items.title: Consumer affairs office
items.text: A provincial or territorial office that gives consumer information and may take complaints about regulated businesses.

items.title: Limitation period
items.text: A time limit, set by province or territory, on when a creditor may use certain court remedies. It is separate from how long a credit report keeps information.

quiz.question: True or False: “Every collector in Canada follows the federal bank rules.”

questions: Who called, from which agency, at what number, and when?
Who was the money first owed to, how much do they say you owe, and when did the debt begin?
How did you verify the caller on your own, and what did you find?
Is the debt yours, unfamiliar, already paid or the wrong amount? Say why in a few words.
Which script will you use, and if the debt is valid, what payment can you afford?
Where will you complain or report, and when will you follow up?
